Adam Stenavich.blurb: Stenavich's four seasons in Green Bay don't show a system built around any single aggressive lever — motion at 47%, play-action at 20%, and tempo at 75 plays per game all land near league average. The one mild outlier is RPO usage at 3%, modestly above the 2% norm. What stands out is the output: +0.06 EPA/play, well above the league average of -0.01, ranking 14th of 82 — though with Jordan Love developing across this window, how much of that belongs to the scheme versus the quarterback is a fair question.

Andy Reid.blurb: Reid's KC offense over this stretch is genuinely pass-heavy — fifth in pass rate over expected at +5.7, against a league average that actually leans run — and leans on screens (10% vs. a 7% norm) and RPOs (4%, third in the league) to manufacture easy looks and stress defenders horizontally. Pre-snap motion runs above average at 50% of snaps. The scheme value sits around league middle, though with moderate reliability given how difficult it is to untangle Reid's system from Mahomes; the honest read is that the style is distinctive, but how much the design itself is generating the +0.06 EPA/play remains an open question.

Ben Johnson.blurb: Ben Johnson's offense is defined above all by play-action — 26% of dropbacks, fourth in the league against an 18% norm — paired with a creativity score that ranks seventh overall, and the results back it up: +0.09 EPA/play, ninth best in the league. His pass tendency sits right at the pack and motion is only modestly above average, so this isn't a system built on pre-snap chaos; it earns its edge through play-design and execution after the snap. Scheme value of +0.106 ranks third among 82 callers, which means the system itself is generating real worth independent of personnel.

Brian Schottenheimer.blurb: Schottenheimer's Dallas offense is almost entirely middle-of-the-pack across the board — motion at 44%, play-action at 20%, tempo at 81 plays per game, all sitting within a few points of league norms. The results were modestly positive at +0.05 EPA/play, but the system ran through one quarterback for essentially the entire window, so there's no clean way to say how much of that belongs to the scheme and how much belongs to the signal-caller.

Drew Petzing.blurb: Petzing's Detroit offense sits near the middle of nearly every structural measure — motion at 36% (below the 41% norm), play-action at 22% (slightly above the 18% average), RPOs essentially absent at 1%, and tempo and screen rate both right at league average. The honest read is that there's no signature wrinkle driving results here; it's a fairly conventional system that produces above-average EPA (+0.03 vs. -0.01 league average) through execution rather than scheme design, with a scheme value that lands squarely in the middle of the pack.

Jim Bob Cooter.blurb: Cooter's Indianapolis offense leaned on play-action (23%, against a league norm of 18%) and RPOs (3%, slightly above the 2% average) more than most, but otherwise sat close to the middle on nearly every other dimension — motion at exactly the league average, tempo and screens both unremarkable. The results matched the profile: -0.02 EPA/play, essentially league average and ranking 45th of 82. A system that asked more of its pre-snap design than its raw pass volume, without much to show either way for it.

Kellen Moore.blurb: Moore's system sits close to league average on nearly every surface metric — pass tendency, play-action, screens, and creativity all within a point or two of normal. The clearest deviation is pre-snap motion, at 50% of dropbacks against a 41% league norm, and his scheme value lands at +0.023 against a league average of -0.012, suggesting the system generates real QB-adjusted value even when the raw EPA (-0.02) looks unremarkable.

Kevin O'Connell.blurb: O'Connell's offense reads as more creative than most — 56th percentile on exoticness, with play-action at 24% against an 18% league norm — but the results haven't backed it up: -0.06 EPA/play ranks 58th, and QB-adjusted scheme value sits at -0.049 against a league average of -0.012. Everything else — motion, tempo, RPOs, screens — lands right at the middle of the pack. The creativity is real; the system just isn't generating surplus value yet.

Kyle Shanahan.blurb: Shanahan's system ranks first in scheme value among the 82 coaches in this index — +0.124 against a league average of -0.012 — and the clearest structural reason is pre-snap motion, which he runs on 60% of dropbacks, nearly 20 points above the ~41% league norm and elite by any measure. Everything else sits close to average: play-action at 18%, tempo at 74 plays per game, screens and RPOs barely registering. The creativity score of 56 reflects genuine but not extreme exoticism; the edge comes from relentless pre-snap manipulation, not from calling unusual plays.

Matt LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur's system shows up as genuinely productive — +0.116 scheme value, indicative of a top-tier system, though with a caveat worth naming: it's difficult to fully untangle from the quarterback he's had, so treat that number as a strong signal rather than a settled verdict. What's notable is how unremarkable the style sheet looks: creativity sits at 55 (league average is 50), motion at 47% against a 41% norm, play-action and tempo right at league average. The results come from execution and structure, not from doing anything exotic.

Matt Nagy.blurb: Nagy runs a pass-heavy attack — sitting at +3.3 over expected, ninth-highest in the league against an average that actually leans run — and leans on RPOs more than almost anyone, at 4% versus a 2% norm. Everything else sits close to league average: motion at 47% (just above the 41% norm), play-action slightly below it, tempo unremarkable. The scheme value of +0.021 is indicative of something functional, but with moderate reliability it's better read as a directional signal than a verdict — the results, +0.04 EPA/play, land in a similar place.

Mike LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur's clearest fingerprint is pre-snap motion — 53% of dropbacks, well above the league's 41% norm — which he uses to stress defenses before the snap rather than through schematic complexity, which sits right at the league average. Play-action is a modest lean at 22% versus 18% league average, and he almost never touches RPOs. The results land above average at +0.04 EPA/play, but because this system ran with effectively one quarterback, separating LaFleur's contribution from his QB's is something the data can't honestly do.

Mike McDaniel.blurb: McDaniel runs one of the most structurally exotic offenses in the league — pre-snap motion on 60% of dropbacks and screens on 11% of plays both rank top-six, against norms of 41% and 7%, and the overall creativity score sits third of 82 coaches. The catch is that the system's QB-adjusted scheme value comes in at -0.055, below the league average of -0.012 and 30th overall, which means all that complexity isn't generating surplus value once you control for quarterback and opponent. He also runs the ball more than most, sitting 5.1 points below expected pass rate.

Sean McVay.blurb: McVay's offense runs on pre-snap manipulation — 54% of dropbacks involve motion, well above the 41% league norm — paired with a play-action rate of 23% against an 18% average. The rest of the profile is fairly conventional: tempo, pass tendency, and screens all sit near league average, and he almost never runs RPOs (1% vs. 2% norm). Scheme value comes in at +0.061, meaningfully above average, though the reliability is only moderate given the quarterback context, so treat it as directionally encouraging rather than definitive.

Sean Payton.blurb: Payton's Denver offense sits at league average on nearly every structural dimension — creativity, tempo, play-action, motion all right at the norm — but two things stand out: screens at 10% (well above the 7% league average) and an RPO rate of 3% (also above average), suggesting a system that creates easier decisions at the point of attack rather than complicating defenses pre-snap. The scheme value of +0.024 against a league average of -0.012 is legitimately above average, though results land right at the EPA mean, which means the system is earning more than it's showing on the scoreboard so far.

Shane Steichen.blurb: Steichen runs a play-action-heavy system — 23% rate against an 18% league average — with slightly elevated RPO usage, and the results in scheme value are genuinely strong: +0.039 against a league average of -0.012, good for ninth out of 82 coaches. Most other dimensions sit right at the norm: motion, tempo, screens, and creativity are all middle-of-the-pack. The honest caveat is that raw offensive EPA comes in slightly below average, so the scheme is generating value above what the personnel and opponents would predict, but the on-field results haven't fully followed yet.

Todd Monken.blurb: Todd Monken runs one of the more quietly effective offenses in the league — +0.045 scheme value, eighth among 82 play-callers, and +0.07 EPA/play despite a system that looks almost aggressively ordinary on paper. Motion, play-action, tempo, screen rate — every dial sits right at league average. The value isn't coming from structural wrinkles; it's coming from execution, which is a real thing and worth crediting plainly.

Wes Phillips.blurb: Phillips's most legible trait is a commitment to play-action — 24% of dropbacks, well above the 18% league average — while most other dials sit near the middle: motion, tempo, RPO, and screen rates all land right at the norm. The system leans slightly pass-heavy relative to game scripts but not by much. Results over his four seasons in Minnesota came in below average at -0.06 EPA/play, though separating scheme value from roster and quarterback variance across that stretch is genuinely difficult.

Zac Taylor.blurb: Zac Taylor runs one of the most pass-heavy systems in the league — a +8.4 PROE ranks second among 82 coaches, against a league average near zero — and does it without much pre-snap disguise or play-action, both of which sit right at the norm. The creativity score of 40 puts him in the bottom quarter, meaning the scheme leans on structure and execution over exoticness. That's not a knock: the system grades out at +0.035 in QB- and opponent-adjusted scheme value, tenth overall, which says the design itself is earning something beyond the personnel.

Bobby Slowik.blurb: Slowik's scheme reads as genuinely creative — 58/100 on exoticness puts him ninth of 82 coordinators, well above the league norm — but the results haven't followed, with EPA/play at -0.04 against a league average of -0.01. Everything else sits right at the middle: play-action, motion, tempo, and screen rate are all within a tick of league norms. The scheme-value number (-0.069) is only moderately reliable given the quarterback situation in Miami, so take it as a signal worth watching rather than a verdict.

Brad Idzik.blurb: Brad Idzik runs one of the more vanilla systems in the league — pre-snap motion at 33% sits well below the ~41% norm, screens are used sparingly at 5% against a 7% average, and nearly everything else lands right at the middle of the pack. The scheme-value number (+0.017, vs. a league average of -0.012) is mildly encouraging but comes with a moderate-reliability flag, meaning the QB's role in those results isn't fully untangled. What you're left with is a system that asks its players to execute a fairly straightforward gameplan at average efficiency — which isn't a knock, just an honest description of where it stands.

Dan Pitcher.blurb: Pitcher's system is defined by one thing that stands out from everything else: he passes more than almost anyone in the league, sitting at +8.4 over expected pass rate against a league average of -0.9, the highest mark among the 82 coaches tracked. Everything else — motion, tempo, RPOs, screens, play-action — runs right at or below league average, and the scheme itself scores low on structural creativity. What he runs is conventional; how aggressively he goes to the air is not, and the offense has produced at +0.06 EPA/play, well above the league average of -0.01.

Frank Smith.blurb: Smith's system is defined by two things that genuinely stand out: pre-snap motion on 70% of dropbacks (the highest rate in the sample, against a ~41% league norm) and screens at 13% of plays, more than double the league average. Play-action also runs at 25%, well above the 18% norm. The results landed right around average at +0.01 EPA/play, which is fine but doesn't fully validate the schematic complexity — though it's worth noting he no longer calls the plays himself.

Joe Brady.blurb: Brady's system sits in genuinely rare territory for creativity — 65/100 against a league norm of 50, fourth-highest among 82 play-callers — built primarily on pre-snap motion that shows up on 52% of dropbacks versus the ~41% league average. Everything else is close to ordinary: play-action, tempo, screen rate, and pass tendency all land right around the mean. The results are elite (+0.18 EPA/play, second overall), though the scheme value of +0.023 comes with a caveat — with one quarterback driving most of this sample, how much belongs to the system and how much to the player isn't fully separable yet.

Joe Lombardi.blurb: Lombardi's Denver offense leaned on a few tools that stand out: play-action at 24% (well above the 18% league norm), screens at 12% (nearly double the 7% average), and RPOs at 4% (also high), suggesting a system built around getting the ball out quickly and keeping defenses off-balance at the line. Everything else — motion, tempo, overall pass tendency — sat right at or near league average. The results were essentially break-even at +0.00 EPA/play, which is fine but doesn't demand a strong read either way.

Klint Kubiak.blurb: Kubiak's system sits in the middle of the pack on most dimensions, but pre-snap motion is the real signature — 50% of dropbacks, well above the 41% league norm, and it shows up as a genuine structural commitment rather than situational decoration. Everything else — play-action, tempo, screens, RPO usage — lands right at league average, and the results match: EPA/play is exactly at the mean. The scheme value of +0.019 against a league average of -0.012 suggests modest positive worth, but this is a system still finding its footing under a first-time HC.

Liam Coen.blurb: Coen's system sits in the middle of the pack on almost every structural dimension — motion, tempo, play-action, RPOs, screens all land right at league norms — which makes the output numbers striking. The +0.101 scheme value ranks fourth among 82 play-callers, and the offenses he's run have produced +0.10 EPA/play, seventh-best in the sample. The honest read is that this isn't a schematically exotic system; it's one that executes conventional football at an unusually high level.

Nathaniel Hackett.blurb: Hackett's system in Arizona was notably conventional by design — pre-snap motion at 30% against a league norm of 41%, almost no RPO usage, and a creativity score of 38 out of 100 that ranks 73rd of 82 coordinators. Everything else — tempo, play-action, pass tendency, screens — sits right at league average. The results were poor (-0.10 EPA/play, well below the -0.01 average), but a minimalist system executed badly isn't the same as a bad concept; what's harder to defend is that the scheme offered little structure to lean on when things went sideways.

Press Taylor.blurb: Press Taylor's system reads almost entirely conventional — motion at 32% against a 41% league norm is the one meaningful deviation, and it runs the other direction, meaning he's using less pre-snap movement than most coordinators. Everything else sits at or near average: play-action, RPO, screen rate, tempo, pass tendency. The scheme value of +0.033 is indicative of something real, but given how much of this sample ran through one quarterback, it can't be cleanly separated from the player.

Zac Robinson.blurb: Robinson's most defining tendency is a strong lean toward the run — he passes 6.3 percentage points below expectation, making him one of the more run-heavy play-callers in the league against a norm of roughly neutral. Beyond that, most of the dials are close to average: tempo, screens, RPOs, and pre-snap motion all sit near the middle of the pack. The scheme value of -0.069 against a league average of -0.012 isn't encouraging, but with a limited sample and a young system still finding its footing, the honest read is that there isn't enough here yet to separate the scheme from its circumstances.

Alex Van Pelt.blurb: Van Pelt's Patriots ran the fastest tempo in the sample — 86 plays per game against a league average of 75 — and leaned on screens at a slightly above-average 9%, but almost everything else sits at or below the norm: conventional motion, ordinary play-action, almost no RPOs. The volume didn't produce value. At -0.11 EPA/play and a QB-adjusted scheme grade of -0.056 against a league average of -0.012, the system ranked near the bottom regardless of pace.

Arthur Smith.blurb: Arthur Smith's Pittsburgh offense runs a bit heavier on play-action (23%, against an 18% league average) and screens (10% vs. 7%), two tools that lean on play-fake credibility and quick distribution — sensible complements to a run-first tendency that sits about 2.5 points below expected pass rate. Everything else — creativity, motion, tempo — is essentially at the league mean, and the results (EPA/play at -0.01) match average too. The scheme value of +0.020 suggests a modest positive above what the quarterback and opponents would predict, but this is a system that earns its keep through identity, not invention.

Declan Doyle.blurb: Doyle's Baltimore offense sits near the top of the league in both creativity and results — a +0.08 EPA/play ranks 11th, and scheme value comes in at +0.052 against a league average of -0.012, though that number carries only moderate reliability given the quarterback involved. What's notable is how little of the exotic shows up in the surface stats: motion, tempo, play-action, and RPO usage all land right at league average. The creativity score of 62 (league avg 50) suggests the exoticness lives in structural design — formations, concepts, or packaging — rather than in the tendencies most systems track.

Doug Nussmeier.blurb: Nussmeier's offense in New Orleans was about as close to baseline as it gets — pass tendency, tempo, RPO usage, and pre-snap motion all sitting right around league average. The one real outlier is screens, which he used at roughly half the league rate (4% vs. 7%), and play-action was notably light at 13% against an 18% norm. Results landed below average at -0.06 EPA/play, though on a Saints roster that was short on talent those two seasons, it's hard to pin that squarely on the scheme.

Eric Bieniemy.blurb: Bieniemy's Kansas City offense passed more aggressively than almost any system in the window — +6.5 over expected pass rate, fourth-highest among 82 coordinators — while running slightly above-average screen usage and otherwise sitting at or below the middle of the pack on motion, play-action, tempo, and creativity. The results were roughly league-average on EPA/play, though what that number actually reflects is genuinely unclear: this scheme operated with one quarterback throughout, and the model can't separate what Bieniemy built from what Mahomes produced.

Grant Udinski.blurb: Udinski's Jacksonville offense was mostly conventional — motion, play-action, tempo, and screen usage all sit right at or slightly below league norms — but the one real deviation is a meaningful lean toward passing, running about 3.5 percentage points more often than expected given game situations, against a league average that actually skews run-heavy. The results were strong: +0.09 EPA/play ranked eighth across 82 play-callers, though Udinski no longer calls the plays himself, so that number now belongs more to context than to his current role.

Greg Roman.blurb: Greg Roman's system is defined by play-action — 27% of dropbacks, second in the league against an 18% norm — paired with pre-snap motion on 52% of snaps, well above the 41% average. Everything else sits close to league norms: tempo, screens, RPOs, overall pass tendency are all ordinary. The indicative scheme value of +0.032 is worth noting, but this offense ran through a specific quarterback and the two are hard to disentangle, so take that number as a signal rather than a verdict. Results land at +0.01 EPA/play, roughly average.

Josh McDaniels.blurb: McDaniels ran a conventionally structured offense — motion, play-action, tempo, and RPO usage all sitting within a few points of league average — with one notable exception: screens at just 4% against a 7% norm, among the lowest in the league. The results were strong (+0.11 EPA/play, fifth overall), but this system ran with effectively one quarterback, so there's no clean way to separate what the scheme produced from what the QB produced.

Ken Dorsey.blurb: Dorsey's calling card in Cleveland is pace — 85 plays per game, second in the league against a norm of 75, and it's not particularly close. Everything else sits right at league average: motion, play-action, RPOs, screens, and creativity all land within a few ticks of normal. He does pass slightly more than situation would predict, ranking 14th in PROE, but that's a tendency, not a defining philosophy. The results have been middling (-0.04 EPA/play, 51st), and the scheme value sits below average at -0.091 against a league mean of -0.012 — so the speed hasn't translated into a meaningful edge.

Klay Kubiak.blurb: Kubiak's offense ran notably pass-heavy — +2.8 over expected pass rate, well above the league norm of -0.9 — and leaned on pre-snap motion at 52% of snaps versus a ~41% league average, using formation movement as a core tool rather than an accent. RPOs were essentially nonexistent (0% against a 2% norm), which fits a system built on decisive pre-snap reads rather than post-snap optionality. The results were elite: +0.13 EPA/play, third-best in the sample — though with two seasons in San Francisco, separating the scheme's value from the roster beneath it is a fair question to hold onto.

Klayton Adams.blurb: Adams ran one of the more conventional schemes in the league — motion, tempo, play-action, and RPO usage all sat right at league average, with a creativity score essentially at the median. The one real outlier is screens, which he used at 4% against a 7% league norm. What complicates the read is that +0.11 EPA/play ranked sixth among 82 play-callers, but Adams operated with Dak Prescott, and separating the system's value from the quarterback's is genuinely difficult here — the results are real, the attribution isn't clean.

Kliff Kingsbury.blurb: Kingsbury's Washington offense leans heavily on play-action (26%, third in the sample against an 18% norm) and RPOs (4%, second overall against a 2% norm), and runs at a genuinely fast pace — 82 plays per game against a 75-play average. The scheme grades as moderately above-average in adjusted value and scores well on creativity, though both reads come with a caveat: this system operated almost entirely with one quarterback, so the numbers are indicative rather than definitive. The results (+0.07 EPA/play, twelfth overall) are real; how much is scheme and how much is quarterback is the honest question.

Luke Getsy.blurb: Getsy's system runs at genuine pace — 83 plays per game ranks eighth in the league against a 75-play norm — and uses pre-snap motion on 51% of dropbacks, well above the 41% average, so there's real structural activity before the snap. Everything else sits at or near league norms: play-action, RPOs, screens, pass tendency, creativity all land in the middle of the pack. The problem is the output: -0.10 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01, and a scheme value of -0.057 versus the -0.012 norm, meaning the system itself hasn't been generating value even after adjusting for quarterback and opponent.

Mike Kafka.blurb: Kafka's Giants offense runs fast — 83 plays per game ranks ninth in the league against an average of 75 — but pace is about the only thing that separates this system from the mean. Motion, play-action, RPO usage, and screen rate all sit right at league norms, and creativity scores below average at 46 out of 100. The results have been rough: -0.14 EPA/play ranks 73rd of 82, and while QB and opponent context are baked into that adjustment, the scheme itself isn't generating value either, coming in at -0.133 against a league average of -0.012.

Mike McCarthy.blurb: McCarthy's Pittsburgh offense leans pass-heavy — +3.2 over expected, meaningfully above the league norm of -0.9 — but without much structural creativity to support it: motion at 35% and play-action at 12% both run below league average, and overall scheme creativity sits right at the median. The system's adjusted value comes in at -0.071 against a league average of -0.012, and the results back that up at -0.08 EPA/play. More passing than most, less infrastructure than most, and the production reflects the gap.

Nick Caley.blurb: Nick Caley's Houston offense is about as close to league average as a system gets — pass tendency, motion, play-action, and tempo all land right at the norm. The one genuine outlier is screen usage at 4%, well below the 7% league average, suggesting he's not leaning on that release valve. Results are modestly positive at +0.01 EPA/play, though the scheme value of -0.020 reads as a slight drag on that, with the caveat that two seasons of data makes it hard to fully untangle the system from the quarterback.

Nick Holz.blurb: Nick Holz runs a run-heavy, conventionally structured offense — pass rate nearly 6 points below expectation puts him at 70th in the league, and almost nothing else in the scheme deviates meaningfully from the norm. Motion, play-action, tempo, and creativity all sit right around league average. The results have been poor: -0.14 EPA/play ranks 72nd, and the scheme value lands below average at -0.119, suggesting the system itself isn't generating much beyond what the personnel provides.

Shane Waldron.blurb: Shane Waldron's system is largely conventional — creativity, pass tendency, play-action, and motion all sit within a few ticks of league average — with one genuine outlier: screens at 12% of plays, nearly double the league norm of 7%, which puts him in the top four across 82 coaches. That's a real structural commitment, not noise. The results so far are below average (-0.03 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01), and the scheme value ranks 27th, so the screens haven't moved the needle enough to offset a system that isn't generating much elsewhere.

Tim Kelly.blurb: Tim Kelly's Giants offense runs fast — 82 plays per game against a league average of 75 — and leans heavily on play-action (24% vs. 18% norm) and screens (10% vs. 7% norm), which together paint a picture of a coordinator trying to manufacture easy throws. The run skew is real: he's passing 4.3 points below expectation, one of the more pronounced tendencies in the league. Scheme value and results both land right around average, which is about what the underlying style suggests — a fairly conventional system executing at a middling level.

Tommy Rees.blurb: Rees runs one of the more run-heavy systems in the league — passing 6 points below expectation, ranking 68th — and strips out nearly every pre-snap wrinkle: motion at 34% against a 41% norm, zero RPOs against a 2% average. The style is conventional by almost every measure, which isn't inherently a problem, but the results are: -0.12 EPA/play ranks 69th, and the QB-adjusted scheme value sits below average at -0.182. Plain execution hasn't made up for the lack of stress on defenses.

Andrew Janocko.blurb: Janocko's one season calling plays in Las Vegas was notably stripped down — play-action at 11% against an 18% league norm, screens at 4% versus 7%, RPOs essentially nonexistent, and one of the slower tempos in the sample at 63 plays per game. The overall creativity score sits right at the middle of the pack, but the consistent lean away from pre-snap and after-snap wrinkles gives the system a conventional, grind-it-out character. Results landed exactly at league average EPA/play, so the approach didn't hurt, but it didn't generate an edge either.

Brian Angelichio.blurb: Angelichio ran a bare-bones drop-back offense in Pittsburgh — almost no motion (22%, against a ~41% norm), minimal play-action (8% vs. 18% league average), and a deliberately slow pace (62 plays per game vs. 75). The one genuine outlier was pass tendency: he called passes at the sixth-highest rate in the sample, well above expectation. The results landed just below average at -0.05 EPA/play, though one season with one roster makes it hard to draw firm conclusions about the scheme's ceiling.

Brian Daboll.blurb: Daboll's offense in Tennessee runs well below league norms across nearly every dimension — passing rate, play-action at 10% against an 18% average, pre-snap motion at 20% against 41%, screens at 3% against 7%, and a tempo of just 54 plays per game against a league average of 75. The result was -0.14 EPA/play, notably below the league average of -0.01. Whether that reflects the scheme or the quarterback running it can't be cleanly separated, so what this data actually describes is a slow, run-heavy, low-concept system that didn't produce at the rate it needed to.

Brian Fleury.blurb: Fleury runs one of the league's more deliberately stripped-down offenses — well below average in tempo (63 plays/game vs. a 75 league norm), motion (25% vs. 41%), play-action (11% vs. 18%), and pass tendency — a system that leans on execution over variety. The creativity score (58/100, top 10 league-wide) suggests some structural wrinkles exist within that framework, but the results land right around middling at -0.04 EPA/play. What the numbers can't answer is how much of that reflects Fleury's design versus his quarterback, and with effectively one QB over the entire window, that question stays open.

Chip Kelly.blurb: Kelly's Las Vegas offense stands out for two things: pre-snap motion on 56% of dropbacks and play-action on 25% of snaps, both well above league norms of 41% and 18% respectively. Everything else — tempo, pass tendency, RPO usage — sits right at the average. The scheme-value estimate is indicative at best given the quarterback situation, but the results were poor regardless: -0.21 EPA/play ranked 76th of 82, which is hard to separate from personnel but hard to ignore.

Dave Canales.blurb: Canales runs a conventionally structured offense — pre-snap motion, pass tendency, and screens all sit right at league average, and his creativity score (40/100) lands near the bottom of the league. The two genuine deviations are tempo (81 plays/game, among the faster offenses in the sample) and RPO usage (4%, well above the 2% norm). Results were essentially league-average at -0.02 EPA/play, but the system ran with one quarterback throughout, so there's no clean way to separate what the scheme produces from what the quarterback provided.

David Blough.blurb: Blough's offense in Washington runs remarkably stripped-down — pre-snap motion at 24% and play-action at 10% both sit well below league norms of 41% and 18%, and the team essentially never uses RPOs or screens. The pace is slow too, at 63 plays per game against a 75-play league average. The scheme value reads as slightly above average, but with only one season of data that number is indicative at best. Results landed right at league average, which for a minimalist system means execution is doing the work.

Davis Webb.blurb: Webb's one season calling plays in Denver was about as stripped-down as it gets — 23% pre-snap motion against a league norm of 41%, play-action at 10% against 18%, and one of the slowest tempos in the league at 57 plays per game. The offense was conventional by almost every measure and produced middling results at –0.04 EPA/play. One season, one quarterback situation — not enough data to draw firm conclusions about scheme value, just a clear picture of what the style was: static, deliberate, and light on manufactured advantages.

Frank Reich.blurb: Reich's Jets offense was about as stripped-down as it gets: pre-snap motion at 18% against a league norm of 41%, play-action at 9% against 18%, and one of the slowest tempos in the sample at 57 plays per game. The scheme ran almost entirely through one quarterback, so there's no clean way to separate Reich's contribution from the player's — the +0.01 EPA/play sitting around league average is a result, not a verdict on the system itself.

John Morton.blurb: Morton's Detroit offense leans heavily on pre-snap motion (59%, against a ~41% league norm) and play-action (26%, well above the 18% average), and it plays fast — 82 plays per game ranks 12th. Screens are also a genuine part of the menu at 10%, nearly 50% above league average. The results look strong at +0.08 EPA/play, but this system ran with one quarterback throughout, so there's no clean way to separate what the scheme produces from what the QB produced.
